title: generosity
hook: generosity — the first practice taught to beginners, not the last

segments.voice: Yesterday: the precepts, five training rules that give others freedom from fear. Your line was do less harm. Which one did you keep? Day fourteen.

Two weeks. Look back at this one. The fourth truth, the path. Sati, remembering to notice. The bell. Anicca, this passes. Anatta, who's in there. The precepts. That's deep water for week two. So you might expect the next word to be even deeper, some advanced meditation. It isn't. In the discourses, it's often the thing the Buddha taught first, to people who had never heard him before. Before the four truths. Before meditation. A monk at dawn, barefoot, holding an empty bowl, walks past a row of houses. Someone steps out with rice. Today, the first practice.
screen: `TWO WEEKS ON YOUR STRAND.` → `AN EMPTY BOWL AT DAWN.` → `THE PRACTICE THAT COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Dana. Giving. Generosity. When the Buddha taught people who were new to his teaching, the discourses say he often followed an order, a gradual talk. He started with giving. Then conduct. Then the good results those bring. Only when someone's heart was ready did he teach the four truths. Giving came first. Not because it's easy, but because it loosens the grip. You can't give with a closed hand. There's a line in the discourses that goes roughly like this: if people knew, as I know, the fruit of giving and sharing, they wouldn't eat without giving, and they wouldn't let stinginess take root. Even their last bite, they'd share, if there were someone to share it with. And the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation, says: "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!" Liberality. Generosity. The answer to greed isn't a lecture. It's a gift. You can still see dana every morning in Thailand, Laos, Myanmar and Sri Lanka. Monks walk with their bowls, and people give food. And a detail: in the Theravada tradition, monks don't ask, and they don't store food for tomorrow. They depend on the giving. And the one who gives is usually understood to receive something too: merit, joy, a lighter heart. In both Theravada and Mahayana lists of the perfections a buddha develops, generosity stands first. Not the last step. The first one.
screen: `DANA — GIVING.` · `THE GRADUAL TALK STARTS HERE.` · `OVERCOME THE GREEDY BY LIBERALITY.` · `THE BOWL AT DAWN.` · then, large: `GIVE FIRST.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Open your hands, palms up, on your knees. Feel what an open hand is like. Now think of one thing you could give today. It doesn't have to be money. Time. Attention. A compliment you've been holding back. The last cookie. Hold that gift in your open hands, and picture the person receiving it. The bell holds the time.
Dana. Giving, generosity: the first practice taught to beginners, and the first of the perfections. Fourteenth word, and two weeks done.
Your line: give first. Today, before you ask anyone for anything, give something first: a thank-you, a coffee, a minute of listening. Day fourteen.

screen: `DAY 14 COUNTS. WEEK TWO, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: SLOW, ON PURPOSE, GOING NOWHERE.`

howItsDone: Buddhists practice dana by offering food, robes and medicine to monastics, most visibly on the morning alms round in Theravada countries, and by giving to others in daily life; temples rely on donations, and some meditation teachers teach freely on a dana basis.

fork.setup: the Buddha meets someone who has never heard his teaching. what does he usually talk about first, in the gradual talk?
fork.reveal: giving came first, then conduct, then their good results. only when the listener was ready did he teach the four truths.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: giving, a gift. The first of the perfections (pāramī).

trapdoor: what you thought: donating to charity.
what it means: generosity as the first practice, the open hand that makes the rest of the path possible.

what a scholar hears: dāna begins the anupubbī-kathā, the gradual talk, and heads the ten pāramīs of Theravada and the six pāramitās of Mahayana. Itivuttaka 26 says those who knew the fruit of giving would share even their last mouthful.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer opens 'Picture'; cut 'which Buddhists love', 'here's what surprises people' and 'many temples run entirely on donations'; added a source line for the perfections lists that put generosity first. The gradual talk's third step is 'heaven' (sagga) in the texts; the script's 'the good results those bring' is a softening a Keeper may want to restore.
Dhammapada 223 quoted from Max Müller (1881); confirm exact wording.
Itivuttaka 26 paraphrased ('even their last bite'). Confirm.
Gradual talk references (DN 3; Mahavagga I) given from memory; the talk appears in many suttas. Confirm a suitable citation.
Monks not storing food: a Vinaya rule for Theravada monastics; Mahayana monastic practice differs (e.g., cooking in monasteries). The script says 'in the Theravada tradition'. Confirm.
Generosity first in both the ten paramis and the six paramitas: confirm.
